subtitle: Practice reading what your division rewards, recognizes and tolerates, sending clearer signals, listening at scale with clear privacy limits, and changing culture one routine at a time with the people it affects.
audience: For senior leaders, directors and managers of managers who are responsible for the culture of a whole division or large unit, and for anyone preparing to lead at that scale.

lessons.title: What this division rewards in practice
objectives: Compare a division's stated values with what it recognizes, resources and tolerates in practice.
Identify at least two kinds of work your division tends to overlook when it celebrates success.
Describe how fairness in outcomes, processes and communication applies to recognition and assignments.
Distinguish reviewing division-wide patterns from rating or ranking individual staff.
lessons.teaching:
Culture is what people learn from what actually happens around them. Staff watch which work is praised at all-staff meetings, which requests get budget and which shortcuts nobody questions. Those patterns can support or contradict a values statement. Senior leaders influence them through attention, resources and responses, alongside the decisions of other people and the conditions of the work.

A useful first step is to compare the stated values with three plain lists. What did we recognize last year, in awards, praise and announcements? What did we resource, in staff time, budget and leadership attention? What did we tolerate, such as late answers to partners, meetings where the same people always speak, or rushed decisions that skipped the people affected? Put each list beside the values the division publishes and ask where they match and where they do not. Keep each list short and concrete; three or four items is enough to start an honest conversation with your managers.

Deloitte's research on inclusive leadership treats fairness as more than identical treatment. It looks at fair outcomes, fair processes and clear communication about decisions, and it names promotions, rewards and work assignments as places where personal and process bias show up. At division scale, ask who is affected by what you reward. Whose work is missing from what you celebrate, perhaps because it is slow, relational or done with partners? How would you find out without relying only on the people already closest to leadership?

Start with your own defaults. Consider whether your own experience has taught you to reward speed, visible output or confidence in meetings. They can be good things, and they can also hide careful work, partnership with people who receive services, and contributions from staff who work differently. The Center for Creative Leadership's REAL framework begins with Reveal: discovering how your own organization works, including norms that often go unnoticed, before choosing what to change. Its other elements, Elevate equity, Activate diversity and Lead inclusively, work alongside Reveal as complementary lenses, not stages to pass through. Use this exercise to review division practices, not to rate individuals from group patterns. That does not replace responsible management of individual concerns. Promotion, pay and selection follow applicable authority, criteria and processes with Human Resources; leaders remain accountable for their own decisions. Required equity analysis and reporting duties continue alongside the exercise.
lessons.keyPoint: A division learns its real values from what its leaders recognize, resource and tolerate. Compare those three lists with what you say you value before you write another values statement.
lessons.example: Practice case: Tomasz is deputy director over waiver policy in disability services. The division's values say that people who receive services shape the work. At the last three all-staff meetings, recognition went to teams that cleared backlogs fastest. A team that spent six months redesigning a notice with self-advocates was not mentioned, and its request for paid advisor time was cut. Imani, who manages that team, raises it with Tomasz and brings examples.
lessons.question: What should Tomasz do first?
choices: Add a recognition category for partnership work at the next all-staff meeting, name Imani's team as its first recipient and ask managers for nominations.
Review with his managers what last year's recognition, funding and tolerated shortcuts said, set it beside the values, and pick one gap to close.
Thank Imani, restate the values at the next all-staff meeting and ask his managers to recognize partnership work more often.
feedback: Recognizing the team is welcome, but a new award alone leaves the funding cut and the pattern behind it untouched. Other overlooked work may stay invisible.

This is the strongest start for reviewing division practices. Imani’s example raises a question about a possible pattern; it does not prove the cause. Review the three signals and the reasons for funding decisions, then identify an authorized change with the people affected.
Restating the values is sincere but adds words, not change. Staff will still judge the values by what is funded and praised, and Imani's concern stays unanswered.
lessons.reflection: What did you personally praise or fund in the last month? What would a new staff member conclude your division values from that alone?
lessons.action: Before your next leadership meeting, list what you recognized, resourced and let slide in the past quarter. Put the lists beside your division's stated values and mark one place where they do not match.

check.question: A division wants to know whether its culture matches its stated values. Which evidence tells it the most?
check.correct: What it has recognized, funded and tolerated over the past year, set beside the values.
wrong: How strongly managers say they agree with the values when asked at a leadership retreat.
Whether every unit has posted the values statement and discussed it at a team meeting.
check.feedback: Culture shows in practice. Agreement with the values and visible statements matter less than what leaders actually reward, resource and let pass, which is what staff watch and learn from.

lessons.title: The signals a senior leader sends every week
objectives: Identify the signals your attention, decisions and visibility choices send across a division.
Use intercultural examples to compare ways of being heard before a decision without assessing an organization’s orientation.
Describe two ways to widen whose knowledge is heard before a division-level decision.
Distinguish access to experience and visibility from formal selection and promotion requirements.
lessons.teaching:
Senior leaders send signals whether or not they mean to. What you ask about in meetings tells managers what matters. What you fund, delay or cut tells them what is real. Who briefs executives or leads cross-division work tells staff what kind of person gets ahead here, and who is heard before a decision tells them whose knowledge counts. Small choices add up, because a whole division is watching them.

Minnesota Management and Budget's leader competency guide describes how leaders send signals across a whole organization. At its in-progress stage, a leader shares successes with a key group only and relies on limited data sources without seeking diverse opinions. A proficient leader builds trust through follow-through and transparent communication, and draws on feedback from collaborators and community leaders. Each of these can be checked against your own calendar and decisions.

Examples from the Intercultural Development Continuum can help examine a meeting format. A Minimization example offers everyone the same fast question-and-answer session without asking what access or preparation it requires. An Acceptance example recognizes that people have different needs and ways of contributing. An Adaptation example changes the format: materials arrive early, written questions are welcomed and needed communication support is arranged with participants. These are illustrations, not assessments of a person, team or organization. Offering several formats also does not establish that every participant can use them; check what is needed and whether the changes work.

To read your own signals, review a month of meetings and recent decisions about budgets or presentations. Look at which roles and units have opportunities, and ask what assumptions shaped those choices. The National Equity Project contrasts a directive approach for problems with known solutions with shared inquiry for complex problems whose solutions must be developed. Its framework does not make every directive decision wrong or remove formal accountability. Ask willing staff what helps or prevents them from contributing, and examine criteria, workload and access with responsible managers. Visibility is not a promise of promotion. Change an authorized meeting format, explain why and review who can participate.
lessons.keyPoint: Staff read a senior leader's calendar, budget and choice of presenters as the real values statement. Changing how opportunity is offered sends a stronger signal than any speech.
lessons.example: Practice case: Graciela directs a division that works with county human services agencies. Each month two of her managers brief the commissioner's office in a fast question-and-answer format, with no materials sent ahead. Program leads write most of the analysis the managers present. One of them, Kwame, is Deaf and works with interpreters, who are rarely booked for these briefings. Recent survey comments say the same voices are always the ones heard. Graciela can change the briefing format and arrange the requested interpreter support. Kwame wants to present his work; access arrangements will follow his needs and applicable requirements.
lessons.question: What should Graciela do?
choices: Invite Kwame to present his own analysis at next month's briefing, and make sure an interpreter is booked for that session.
Keep the current presenters, since the briefings go well, credit the program leads by name on every slide and invite them to observe the briefings.
Rotate presenters on criteria shared in advance, send materials ahead, book interpreters by default and let authors brief their own work.
feedback: Arrange the needed access for Kwame’s next briefing promptly; it is a responsibility, not a favor. A single invitation alone leaves the recurring format and opportunity criteria unchanged. Improve those too without delaying his access.
Credit matters, but observing does not provide the same opportunity to explain one’s own analysis. Ask authors about participation and support, and examine why only the current managers present.

This is the strongest overall response in this case. It improves the recurring format and makes opportunity criteria visible while providing needed support. Confirm arrangements with participants; rotation and advance materials alone do not guarantee access or fair outcomes.
lessons.reflection: In the last month, which roles and units reached senior leaders directly, and which arrived through someone else? What habit of yours shaped that?
lessons.action: Review the last three months of your calendar and leadership briefings. Note which units, roles and ways of contributing appear, then change one format so more people can bring their own work forward.

check.question: Which briefing arrangement best illustrates Adaptation in this example, without assessing anyone’s orientation?
check.correct: Authors brief their own work, with materials, written questions and interpreters arranged ahead.
wrong: Anyone may speak, and the same fast question-and-answer format is used for every briefing.
Leaders agree that the format favors quick talkers and plan to discuss it at a retreat.
check.feedback: Using one format for everyone can favor one style. Noticing that is a real step. Adaptation goes further: it changes the routine itself and then checks whether it worked.

lessons.title: Listening at scale with clear privacy limits
objectives: Explain the protections and use limits described for the 2025 enterprise survey, distinguishing them from local listening sessions.
Plan a way to discuss results with staff that does not try to trace any comment to a person.
Describe how stay conversations can inform themes while preserving necessary records and reporting duties.
Draft a short report back that states what will change, what will not and why.
lessons.teaching:
A division learns about work through surveys, stay conversations and concerns people raise directly. Each source shows part of the picture, and none guarantees that everyone has been heard. Plan how information will be collected, used, stored and shared before inviting people to contribute. Explain the limits of confidentiality and how required reports will be handled. A useful listening process reduces unnecessary exposure and shows what changed because people contributed.

Minnesota Management and Budget’s FAQ describes the 2025 enterprise engagement and inclusion survey. Management Analysis and Development, or MAD, administered it and knew who responded. Identifying information was protected under state law, with disclosure only as allowed by law. MAD removed identifying information from agency data and combined groups with fewer than 10 respondents. The FAQ says results are not for individual performance evaluations, and the survey is not a misconduct-reporting channel. It recommends sharing results and developing action plans with staff. These are the stated arrangements for that survey; check current guidance before describing another survey’s protections.

Work from the authorized reports and data, and do not try to identify comment authors. A distinctive phrase or small group can reveal someone even after names are removed. Ask responsible survey and data-practices staff what can be shared, then describe themes without unnecessary identifying detail. A low score may prompt inquiry, but it does not establish a particular cause or prove misconduct. Individual concerns still deserve an appropriate response even when no wider pattern is known.

Stay conversations ask what helps a person remain in a role and what might lead them to leave. They do not inherit the enterprise survey’s protections. Tell staff what notes are needed, who may receive them and what confidentiality cannot be promised. Share suitable themes in general discussion while retaining necessary records under applicable rules. Do not omit a required report, destroy records or promise that no information about individuals will be kept. A facilitator outside the reporting line may help participation, but a group session cannot guarantee anonymity.

Report back on what you learned, what you can change, what you cannot change and when you will update staff. Consider whose experience is missing and offer accessible ways to contribute without pressure to disclose personal details. Follow the reporting duties for your role. HR/LR Policy 1436 requires managers and supervisors to report protected-class harassment or discrimination allegations immediately to the designated office. Follow DHS referral and consultation procedures rather than investigating through a listening session. Address urgent danger through the applicable emergency or safety route; do not wait for a survey cycle or an action-plan meeting.
lessons.keyPoint: Explain privacy limits before gathering feedback, share only appropriate information, follow reporting duties and tell staff what their input changed.
lessons.example: Practice case: Mariam is deputy director over licensing in disability services. In the 2025 enterprise survey, one licensing unit of about 20 staff scored low on inclusion items, and several written comments describe meetings where questions are brushed aside. Paolo, a manager in another area, suggests matching the comments to people in the unit so each concern can be handled directly. The unit's manager is worried and asks Mariam what happens next. The released report contains themes authorized for this discussion. Any concern requiring immediate action or formal referral will be handled separately under the applicable procedure.
lessons.question: What should Mariam do?
choices: Share the unit's themes with its staff, hold listening sessions led by someone outside the reporting line, and report back within a month.
Ask the unit's manager to meet each staff member privately to learn what is behind the comments and resolve the concerns.
Wait for the next survey cycle to see whether the pattern holds before acting, so the unit is not singled out on the strength of one result.
feedback: This is the strongest planning response under the stated conditions. Share appropriate themes, explain the sessions’ confidentiality limits and offer other ways to contribute. An outside facilitator does not guarantee anonymity, and reporting duties continue. The month is a report-back target, not a delay for urgent action.
One-to-one meetings can feel like a search for the authors, especially with the manager the comments describe. People may say less next time, and trust in the survey drops.
Caution about one result is reasonable, but a long silence tells staff their answers changed nothing. A modest, honest response now keeps the next survey worth answering.
lessons.reflection: When you have said something honest at work, what told you it was safe and worth it? What will your staff see from you after the next survey?
lessons.action: Using results you are authorized to access and share, choose one theme and draft a report back. State what you learned, what can change, what cannot change and why, and when you will update staff. Check the draft for details that could identify someone.

check.question: Under the 2025 enterprise survey FAQ, which use of released results supports improvement without identifying respondents?
check.correct: Looking for themes across groups and building an action plan with the staff who answered.
wrong: Using comments about one manager's meetings as evidence in that manager's performance review.
Sharing every written comment word for word with all staff so that nothing is filtered.
check.feedback: Use themes to plan improvements with staff, including willing contributors who answered and those whose experience may be missing. Do not determine who answered or use these results for individual performance evaluations. The 2025 FAQ directs misconduct concerns to HR or agency procedures. Sharing every comment can expose identities.

lessons.title: Changing culture one routine at a time
objectives: Select one division routine where stated values and daily practice clearly differ, and plan its redesign.
Plan how the staff, partners and people served who use that routine will help redesign it.
Define what you will look at, for whom and when, to check whether the change worked.
Identify when a culture change needs Human Resources or labor relations involved.
lessons.teaching:
Culture change needs follow-through in daily work. A values campaign can explain a direction, but it does not by itself change how people experience the work. A changed routine, such as how work is assigned, how a meeting runs or how a partner's question gets answered, changes what people do every week. Over time, what people do becomes what the division is. Leaders often reach for visible launches because they show commitment quickly; the harder work is changing the ordinary steps people repeat.

The United States Office of Personnel Management built a federal inclusion measure on the idea that repeated behaviors form inclusive habits. Its 2017 report, now historical, said individual behaviors repeated over time create an inclusive work environment, and grouped those habits as fair, open, cooperative, supportive and empowering. This is a useful way to examine practice, not proof that one change will transform a division. Choose a routine where evidence suggests a gap, and propose a feasible improvement within your authority. Set a realistic review period based on the work and the people affected.

Involve the people the routine affects before you redesign it. Ask frontline staff, partners and, where it fits, people who receive services how it works for them now and what would make it better. Decide together what you will look at, for whom and when. Their experience can reveal problems that other evidence misses. Consider it alongside service data and required standards, and explain how their input affects the proposal. The National Equity Project calls this leading from the inside out, in three moves it names See, Engage and Act: understand yourself and the system, make sense of the situation with others, then try small tests with the people affected instead of one large fix. Minnesota Management and Budget's leader competency guide describes expert organizational leaders as explaining the change, monitoring results and adjusting plans. Its expert description for leading others adds disrupting norms and patterns that keep inequities in place.

Give a change enough time and support to learn from it, while monitoring for harm. Set access safeguards, stop conditions and a responsible reviewer before a trial. Do not treat harm as ordinary adjustment or wait for the planned review when action is needed. Review at the times you set: what happened, for whom, and what will you keep, change or stop? Once a change is authorized, update the appropriate procedures and handover records so others can maintain and reassess it. Tell staff and partners what you learned at each review, including what did not work. Before changing duties, schedules or matters covered by a labor agreement, involve Human Resources and labor relations. A small test does not waive these requirements or required agency equity analysis.
lessons.keyPoint: Improve a routine with the people it affects, check what happens for different groups and preserve the approved process with clear responsibility for reviewing it.
lessons.example: Practice case: Beatriz directs a disability services area that works with lead agencies across the state. Last year the area launched five culture initiatives, and most faded within months. Lead agency partners still say their questions wait weeks and get different answers from different staff. Sunil, a program consultant, keeps an informal answer guide that colleagues quietly rely on. A reorganization is expected next spring. Beatriz is now setting priorities for next year. The responsible program staff can authorize a limited improvement before the reorganization. They will verify the informal guide against current policy and monitor access and service problems before the six-month review.
lessons.question: What should Beatriz plan for next year?
choices: Launch a refreshed set of initiatives with a values campaign and a culture committee, backed by stronger communication.
Redesign how partner questions are answered with consultants and lead agency partners, build on Sunil's guide and check at six months.
Pause culture work until the coming reorganization settles, then start again next year with a clear plan once the new structures are known.
feedback: Fresh energy and better communication help, but repeating a pattern that faded last year is likely to fade again, and partners' daily experience stays the same.

This is the strongest plan under the stated conditions. It focuses on a service problem, includes people who use the process and preserves useful knowledge after checking its accuracy. The six-month review supplements ongoing monitoring; it is not a reason to postpone needed corrections.

Some changes may need to wait for authority or a settled structure. Here, a limited improvement is authorized and can address current delays. Coordinate with the reorganization and document what future staff need to review.
lessons.reflection: Which routine in your area would show your stated values most clearly if it changed? What has kept you from changing it so far?
lessons.action: Choose one routine in your area where practice and stated values differ. Invite willing people who use it to describe their experience; a few views will not represent everyone. Propose a change with the required authority, access support, monitoring and review date.

check.question: Which approach is most likely to change a division's culture over time?
check.correct: Redesigning one routine with the people it affects and reviewing what happened at set times.
wrong: Launching several initiatives at once so that staff can see a strong commitment to culture.
Announcing a clear set of values and asking every manager to model them consistently.
check.feedback: Changing a recurring practice and reviewing its effects connects stated values with daily work. Communication and leadership example can support it, but announcements alone do not establish that experience or outcomes have improved.

cards.back: A shortcut or habit leaders see and let pass, such as late answers to partners. What a division tolerates teaches staff as much as what it praises.

The National Equity Project describes circle leadership as shared inquiry for complex problems whose solutions must be developed through learning. It does not replace accountability or make directive action inappropriate in every situation.
Any choice a leader makes that staff read as a message about what matters: what you ask about, fund, delay, praise or let pass.

A conversation about what helps someone remain in a role and what might lead them to leave. Explain the use of notes and privacy limits, share appropriate themes and follow records and reporting duties.
Telling the people who gave feedback what you heard, what you will do, what you will not do and why, and when you will update them again.

aid.heading: Read what your division rewards
items: List what you recognized last quarter: awards, praise and who presented to executives.
List what you resourced: staff time, budget requests approved and your own attention.
List what you tolerated: slow answers to partners and meetings few people can join.
Set all three beside the stated values and mark where they match and where they do not.
Review division practices without rating people from group patterns; respond appropriately to individual concerns through the responsible processes.

aid.heading: Listen with clear privacy limits
items: Read survey results by question and group; never try to work out who wrote a comment.
Explain the use of notes, confidentiality limits and reporting duties before stay conversations or group sessions.
Use the designated reporting routes for discrimination or harassment and the appropriate safety route for urgent danger; do not wait for an action-plan meeting.
Ask who was not heard, such as night shifts, remote staff or units with few respondents.
Report back within a set time: what you heard, will do, will not do and why.

aid.heading: Change one routine and stay with it
items: Pick one routine where the gap between values and practice is clear and widely felt.
Redesign it with the staff, partners and people served who use it.
Before a trial, arrange authority and access support, define what you will check for different groups and set review dates and stop conditions.
Review at those times and decide what to keep, change or stop.
After authorization, update procedures and handover records; consult Human Resources and labor relations before changes to covered duties or schedules.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget, 2025 Enterprise Employee Engagement and Inclusion Survey: Frequently Asked Questions
sources.note: Supports lesson 3 on survey privacy, combining groups under 10, no use for individual evaluations, misconduct going to Human Resources, and sharing results with staff. Describes the 2025 survey only.

sources.title: Deloitte University Press, The six signature traits of inclusive leadership (2016)
sources.note: Supports lesson 1 on fairness in outcomes, processes and communication, and on promotions, rewards and assignments as places bias appears. 2016 consulting research based on interviews with leaders in six countries, mostly outside government.

sources.title: U.S. Office of Personnel Management, 2017 Federal Employee Viewpoint Survey Governmentwide Management Report
sources.note: Supports lesson 4's statement that repeated behaviors form inclusive habits, and the five habits named. A historical federal measure from 2017; pages on the inclusion measure only were read.

sources.title: IDI, LLC, The Intercultural Development Inventory
sources.note: Defines the continuum orientations. Meeting examples illustrate concepts and do not assess individuals, teams or organizations.

sources.title: Center for Creative Leadership, The Research Foundations for REAL: A Framework for Leadership Action in Equity, Diversity and Inclusion (2023)
sources.note: Supports examining organizational norms and using REAL’s four elements as complementary lenses, not stages. A research-informed practitioner framework; the course does not claim that applying it proves local outcomes.

sources.title: National Equity Project, Leading for Equity Framework (2024)
sources.note: Supports lesson 2's contrast of pyramid and circle leadership, the circle leadership card, and lesson 4's inside-out stance of See, Engage and Act with small tests. Copyrighted; ideas paraphrased. A practitioner model written for schools, not outcome research.
